prompt:
Reddit post, r/houseplants.
Title: Please help! Monstera Prop not going well?

Tl;Dr I tried to save my dying monstera by propagating the only healthy looking bits that were left. It's been in a jug of water with spagham moss, water gets changed regularly, it's been 3 weeks and I have no roots yet..

After a week or two of it not recovering, I decided I needed to do emergency surgery. I watched some YouTube videos on propagating monstera and I cut the "middle" section out of the plant, as that's where the "healthiest" looking leaves remained. I used a clean, fresh razor blade to make the cuts and did exactly as the video said... I have changed the water out every 3-4 days. The leaves still look unchanged, no better or worse, but there are no signs of new roots or new growth anywhere and the areas that were cut have just turned brown...

What is wrong with my plant?
answer:
The cuttings are rotting, not failing to root. The black, mushy lesions at the cut ends and along the stems are stem rot, most likely bacterial or fungal, and the rot is probably coming from the parent. Monstera stems are often infected through roots that have started to rot, and cutting into infected tissue spreads it. Your cuttings are also missing a clear node (the bump where a leaf or aerial root emerges), and rot-prone stems in stagnant water can't root.

**How to tell:** Look at the cut ends. If the brown extends into firm, bright green tissue when you slice it, the rot is still spreading. If the tissue is firm and green all the way through, the cut may be salvageable.

**Fix the cuttings:**
- Cut back to clean, firm green tissue, ideally just below a visible node, using a sterilized blade.
- Let the cut ends callus for 1 to 2 days in the air.
- Set them in fresh water, changed every few days, in bright indirect light and warmth. Sphagnum in the jug can hold water and hide rot, so you can skip it.
- Discard any cutting that goes soft again.

**Check the parent plant, which is the real problem:**
- Lift it out of the pot and inspect the roots. Healthy roots are firm and tan or white. Brown, hollow, or mushy roots that slough off mean root rot.
- Trim all rotten roots with sterile scissors and repot in fresh, chunky aroid mix (perlite, bark, and coir or peat) in a pot with drainage holes. Don't leave it sitting in a decorative cachepot with water.
- Water only when the top 2 to 3 inches are dry, and make sure excess water drains out fully.

If the parent's roots are mostly healthy, the stem rot may be coming from somewhere else, so look closely at the base of the plant and any wounds.
